facts.statement: Brighstoneus is a genus of hadrosauriform dinosaur found in the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation on the Isle of Wight, England.
facts.quote: Brighstoneus (after Brighstone, a village on the Isle of Wight) is a genus of hadrosauriform dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, England.

facts.statement: The genus Brighstoneus contains only one known species, Brighstoneus simmondsi, which is known from a partial skeleton.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, Brighstoneus simmondsi, known from a partial skeleton.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen MIWG 6344 was discovered in the summer of 1978 after a storm caused a collapse at Grange Chine.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, MIWG 6344, was discovered along with the holotype of Neovenator during the summer of 1978, when a storm made part of the Grange Chine collapse.

facts.statement: The fossils date to the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: The rocks were part of the plant debris bed L9 within the variegated clays and marls of the Wessex Formation dating from the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, about 125 million years ago.

facts.statement: Remains initially thought to be Iguanodon generated significant interest in the early 1980s, leading to further collection efforts.
facts.quote: The "Iguanodon", later referred to Mantellisaurus, at first generated the most interest and in the early 1980s a team was sent by the NHM to secure more of its bones.

facts.statement: Brighstoneus was identified as distinct from Mantellisaurus in 2019 by Jeremy Lockwood during his PhD research at the University of Portsmouth.
facts.quote: Brighstoneus was found to be distinct from Mantellisaurus by 2019 when being studied by the retired physician Jeremy Lockwood cataloguing all iguanodontian fossils from Wight for his PhD study at the University of Portsmouth.

facts.statement: Brighstoneus simmondsi was formally named and described in 2021 by Jeremy Lockwood, David Martill, and Susannah Maidment.
facts.quote: The new taxon was named and described as the type species Brighstoneus simmondsi by Jeremy Lockwood, David Martill and Susannah Maidment in 2021.

facts.statement: The species name simmondsi honors Keith Simmonds, who assisted in the discovery of the remains.
facts.quote: The specific name honours Keith Simmonds as discoverer.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of a partial skeleton that includes the skull and lower jaws.
facts.quote: The holotype consists of a partial skeleton with skull and lower jaws.

facts.statement: The bones were not articulated and were found intermingled with Neovenator bones over an area of six by five meters.
facts.quote: The bones were not articulated but found intermingled with the Neovenator bones over a surface of six by five metres.

facts.statement: The bones were damaged by beetle larvae before they fossilized.
facts.quote: They had been damaged by beetle larvae prior to fossilisation.

facts.statement: The original description noted that Brighstoneus was large in size but did not provide specific estimates for dimensions or body mass.
facts.quote: In their paper describing Brighstoneus, Lockwood and colleagues did not provide any estimates of dimensions or body mass, though noted that it was large in size.

facts.statement: A 2024 estimate by Gregory S. Paul suggests Brighstoneus was approximately 6 meters long and weighed about 1 ton.
facts.quote: In 2024, Gregory S. Paul estimated that Brighstoneus was probably 6 m in length, and provided a body mass estimate of about 1 t.

facts.statement: Brighstoneus possesses a unique nasal bulla where the nasal bone bulges upward past the nostril opening, a feature rare among iguanodontians.
facts.quote: The skull of Brighstoneus differs from many other iguanodontians in that the nasal bone past the naris (the opening for the nostril and nasal chambers) bulged dorsally (upwards), forming a so-called nasal bulla.

facts.statement: The dorsal surface of the nasal bone in Brighstoneus forms an almost entirely unique "S"-shape when viewed from the side.
facts.quote: The morphology seen in Brighstoneus, wherein the dorsal surface of the nasal would be somewhat "S"-shaped when viewed from the side, was almost entirely unique.

facts.statement: In Brighstoneus, the maxillary process accounts for roughly 60% of the jugal bone's length, a proportion higher than in most hadrosauriforms (40–54%) but similar to Ouranosaurus (62%).
facts.quote: Roughly 60% of the total length of the jugal is taken up by the maxillary process, the structure to which the maxilla would have attached; in most hadrosauriforms, this number is between 40–54%, save for the closely related Ouranosaurus, in which it was 62%.

facts.statement: The predentary bone features a bilobed, heart-shaped process on its underside.
facts.quote: It bore a bilobed, heart-shaped process on its ventral (bottom) aspect.

facts.statement: The dorsal surface of the predentary bone bears a series of large denticles.
facts.quote: On the dorsal surface were a series of large denticles.

facts.statement: The dentary row contains 28 tooth sockets, with a potential additional socket indicated by a small pit on the right dentary.
facts.quote: The dentary row contains 28 alveoli (tooth sockets), with a small pit on the right dentary which may represent another.

facts.statement: Among hadrosauriforms with a system of active and replacement teeth in the same socket, Brighstoneus holds the record for the highest number of alveoli.
facts.quote: Among hadrosauriforms like Brighstoneus, taxa which adopted a system where one active and one replacement crown were found in the same alveolus (in contrast to more derived, later taxa), this is the highest number of alveoli known.

facts.statement: A high ridge ran along Brighstoneus' spine, with neural spines at the tail base exceeding 370% the height of the vertebral centra.
facts.quote: A relatively high ridge ran along much of Brighstoneus' vertebral column, reaching its apex over the base of the tail, where some neural spines were over 370% the height of the vertebral centra (the main bodies of the vertebrae).

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses in 2021 placed Brighstoneus within the clade Iguanodontia.
facts.quote: In 2021, Jeremy Lockwood and colleagues performed a series of phylogenetic analyses which placed Brighstoneus in the Iguanodontia.

facts.statement: Most analyses suggest Brighstoneus is a basal member of Hadrosauriformes, forming a polytomy with Barilium, Hypselospinus, Iguanodon, and Mantellisaurus.
facts.quote: In most analyses, it was found to be more basal in the Hadrosauriformes, in a polytomy with related forms including the British Barilium, Hypselospinus, Iguanodon and Mantellisaurus.

facts.statement: One analysis excluding specific nasal and ilium characters recovered Brighstoneus outside Hadrosauriformes as a sister species to Ouranosaurus.
facts.quote: In an analysis excluding two new characters describing the nasal and ilium, resolution within Hadrosauriformes could be found, with Brightstoneus recovered outside of the Hadrosauriformes as a sister species of Ouranosaurus as seen below.

facts.statement: A 2024 study by Lockwood et al. recovered Brighstoneus as the earliest-diverging member of Hadrosauroidea within Hadrosauriformes.
facts.quote: In their 2024 description of Comptonatus, another Wessex Formation iguanodont, Lockwood and colleagues published an updated version of this phylogenetic matrix, recovering Brighstoneus as the earliest-diverging member of Hadrosauroidea within Hadrosauriformes, rather than as the sister to Ouranosaurus outside of this clade.

facts.statement: A 2025 study by Bertozzo et al. recovered Brighstoneus as the sister taxon to a clade containing Comptonatus and Brighstoneus.
facts.quote: Using a novel phylogenetic matrix for their description of the Portuguese hadrosauroid Cariocecus bocagei, Bertozzo et al. (2025) recovered this taxon as the sister taxon to a clade formed by Comptonatus and Brighstoneus.

facts.statement: These taxa are placed within Hadrosauroidea, having diverged after the Iguanodontidae.
facts.quote: These taxa were placed within the Hadrosauroidea, diverging after the Iguanodontidae.

facts.statement: A 2026 study by Huang et al. using an updated matrix recovered a comparable clade for these taxa.
facts.quote: A study by Huang and colleagues (2026) using an updated version of this matrix recovered a comparable clade.

facts.statement: The holotype of Brighstoneus was found in Barremian deposits of the Wessex Formation.
facts.quote: The holotype of Brighstoneus was collected from strata belonging to the Wessex Formation, more specifically from Barremian deposits.

facts.statement: Brighstoneus lived on a floodplain environment intersected by rivers and lakes.
facts.quote: Sedimentological data suggests that the depositional environment of the Wessex Formation was a floodplain intersected by fluvial (river) and lacustrine (lake) deposits.

facts.statement: Water levels in Brighstoneus's habitat varied seasonally due to high evaporation despite significant precipitation.
facts.quote: Water levels likely varied throughout the year, due to there being more evaporation than precipitation, though precipitation was regardless quite high.

facts.statement: The environment experienced frequent extreme storms and floods that deposited dead organisms in ponds.
facts.quote: The Wessex seems to have regularly experienced extreme storms and periodic flood events, resulting in debris flows which would have deposited dead organisms in ponds.

facts.statement: Frequent wildfires occurred in the habitat, which prevented the dense growth of gymnosperms.
facts.quote: Burned plant and insect material and fusain suggests that the environment experienced frequent wildfires, stifling for the most part the dense growth of gymnosperms.

facts.statement: Brighstoneus belongs to the parent group Hadrosauriformes.
facts.quote: Parent group: Hadrosauriformes

facts.statement: Brighstoneus is classified within the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Brighstoneus is Brighstoneus simmondsi.
facts.quote: Type species: Brighstoneus simmondsi

facts.statement: Brighstoneus lived during the Barremian stage, between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Barremian (125.77 to 121.4 million years ago)

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Brighstoneus has been recorded.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 1
